reply.title: Squashing Infinity: The Logistic Curve
reply.story:
When modeling probabilities or neural networks, we often need to take any real number from negative infinity to positive infinity and squash it neatly into a range between zero and one. Early biometricians and statisticians faced this exact problem when studying population growth, where growth starts exponential but caps out due to limited resources. Pierre François Verhulst introduced a differential equation that naturally produced an S-shaped curve, known today as the logistic function.

The magic of this curve lies in its formula, which uses an exponential term in the denominator. As the input grows extremely large and positive, the exponential term shrinks toward zero, driving the overall fraction to one. Conversely, as the input drops toward negative infinity, the exponential term grows massively, dragging the fraction down toward zero. At the exact midpoint, the output hits one half.

By adjusting the steepness parameter, we can make the transition from zero to one sharp like a switch or gradual like a ramp. The derivative at any point reveals the sensitivity of the output to changes in the input, reaching its maximum slope right at the midpoint. This elegant squashing mechanism turns unbounded inputs into bounded probabilities.
reply.cardDescription: Explore how the logistic function squashes any real input into a strictly bounded range between zero and one. Adjust the steepness, midpoint, and marker position to observe the curve and its slope.
